summary.text:
The second council to give us five PWLB certainty rates that match our own series to the basis point. Derbyshire's outturn prints 1yr 5.04%, 5yr 5.28%, 10yr 5.72%, 20yr 6.23% and 50yr 6.08% for 31 March 2026, and every one ties — including the 20-year, which Shropshire did not quote. Four of their own balance-sheet identities hold exactly as well.

The position is a third short. £124.500m of the £400.929m book is short-term local authority money at 4.46% with a weighted average maturity of 0.20 years, so 33% falls due inside twelve months. Internal borrowing has risen sharply, from £233.405m to £302.830m, and the report says why: reserves have been used to fund the DSG deficit.

Their own liability benchmark is the striking part. Existing borrowing runs down to £267.736m in 2027, £259.044m in 2028 and £215.286m in 2029, while the benchmark rises to £388.178m, £422.435m and £398.332m. That is a gap of roughly £120m, £163m and £183m to be raised across three years — and the resources netted off to get there include an estimated £84.051m SEN Refund in 2026-27. Three officer addresses are published.

officer.subject: Five rates, and what your liability benchmark says next
officer.body:
Hi Jon,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Audit Committee on 15 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

I'll start with a compliment that doubles as our cross-check, because your report made it possible. The context table at the end prints five PWLB certainty rates for 31 March — 1yr 5.04%, 5yr 5.28%, 10yr 5.72%, 20yr 6.23% and 50yr 6.08% — and our own series gives all five for the same day, to the basis point. Only one other council we've read this month quotes five, and they didn't include the twenty-year. Four of your balance-sheet identities tie exactly too, which is rarer than it should be.

So this isn't a note about whether your numbers are right. It's about the shape they describe.

A third of the book — £124.5m of the £400.9m — is short-term local authority money at 4.46% with a weighted average maturity of 0.20 years. That's 33% falling due inside twelve months, well inside your 60% limit but a long way from where most books sit. Internal borrowing has gone from £233.4m to £302.8m in a year, and the report is straightforward about part of the reason: reserves used to fund the DSG deficit.

What caught our eye is your own liability benchmark. Existing borrowing runs down to £267.7m in 2027, £259.0m in 2028 and £215.3m in 2029, while the benchmark rises to £388.2m, £422.4m and £398.3m. That's roughly £120m, £163m and £183m to be raised across three years — and the balance sheet resources netted off to get there include an estimated £84.051m SEN Refund in 2026-27. It's a well-constructed indicator and it's telling you something quite specific about timing.

Where that lands depends on the curve on the day. Two-year certainty money is 5.06% today and five-year 5.34%, so the short end has barely moved since March; the long end has, with fifty-year at 6.27% against your 6.08%. Bank Rate is still 3.75% but the one-year OIS is about 4.11%, so the market is pricing up rather than down.

None of that needs a meeting or a subscription. The rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds, both fixings, whole curve. Your PWLB book priced daily against the DMO repayment curve — premiums and discounts as a lookup rather than a request — is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. And the monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is a useful read on how thin the market is before you roll: July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%.

On training, three fit Derbyshire: our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data and is exactly the indicator your Table 11 is doing; Interest rate risk, for the short-dated third of the book; and Strategic PWLB borrowing, for what comes after 2027. It's worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for the committee this goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
